title: The Arrest Video
subtitle: A clip of a student being dragged into a van is everywhere; nobody can find the student
coldOpen: 19:20. A 12-second clip: a student dragged into a white van.
19:45. The caption says police took him from the hostel.
Five hundred students are at the station gate by eight.

briefing.grievance: Students believe a classmate was taken by police without a record. The station says it has no such person. Either someone is lying, or someone is missing.
knownFacts: The station’s custody register shows no student intake tonight.
The clip is 12 seconds, filmed at night, with no visible badges or plates.
A student named in the caption has not answered his phone since 18:00.
unverifiedClaims: A post names an officer as the one driving the van.
A message says the student is being held at a “black site”.
briefing.responsibility: You run the police station and the campus liaison. A missing student is a real problem; a fake video is another; both need the truth fast.
briefing.objective: Find the student, verify the clip, keep the station gate calm, and do not let either story become the official one without evidence.

rightsMoments.question: Students demand to know whether a classmate is in custody. What are they entitled to?

options.text: Prompt, verifiable information: anyone detained must be recorded, and family or friends told; a denial should be checkable.
options.feedback: Correct. Custody must be recorded and disclosed; secrecy is what makes a fake clip believable.

options.text: Nothing; the police decide what to disclose about custody.
options.feedback: Arrest safeguards require records and notification; they are not optional.

options.text: Only a court can tell them, after a petition.
options.feedback: Courts are a backstop; the duty to record and inform applies immediately.

rightsMoments.principle: Article 22 and arrest guidelines require every detention to be recorded and relatives informed. Transparency about custody is the lawful answer to a rumour of secret arrest.
rightsMoments.why: Opening the register and walking the cells with student representatives did what no loudspeaker denial could.

source.label: Constitution of India, Articles 21 and 22 (India Code)

simple.question: Students want to know if their friend is in custody. What are they owed?

options.a: Quick, checkable answers. Every arrest must be written down and families told.
options.b: Nothing. Police decide what to share.
options.c: Only a court can tell them.

feedback.a: Yes! Arrests must be recorded and shared. Secrecy feeds rumours.
feedback.b: No. Writing down arrests and telling families is the rule.
feedback.c: Courts help later. The duty to tell people starts right away.

simple.principle: Every arrest must be recorded and families told. Openness is the answer to secret-arrest rumours.
simple.why: Showing the register to students did what no loudspeaker denial could.
